clinicalPearls: Cardinal symptoms are unsteadiness worse in the dark or on uneven ground and oscillopsia (bouncing vision) during head movement or walking
Vertigo is usually absent because the deficit is symmetrical, which often delays recognition
A positive bedside head impulse test in both horizontal directions and dynamic visual acuity loss on head shaking are key clinical signs
Causes include aminoglycoside ototoxicity, bilateral Meniere disease, autoimmune and genetic disorders, and many cases remain idiopathic
Formal diagnosis requires demonstrating reduced vestibulo-ocular reflex gain bilaterally on quantitative testing
Vestibular rehabilitation to promote substitution and gaze stabilisation is the mainstay of management
It may occur with progressive cerebellar ataxia and neuropathy in the CANVAS spectrum, warranting neurological assessment
reference.pathophysiology: Bilateral vestibulopathy results from impaired function of both peripheral vestibular organs or their nerves, reducing the vestibulo-ocular and vestibulospinal reflexes that stabilise gaze and posture. Because the loss is symmetrical there is no static imbalance signal to generate spinning vertigo; instead the failure of the vestibulo-ocular reflex causes retinal image slip during head movement, perceived as oscillopsia, and loss of vestibulospinal support causes gait unsteadiness that worsens when vision and proprioception cannot compensate, such as in darkness. Ototoxic aminoglycosides preferentially damage vestibular hair cells, while other cases reflect autoimmune, degenerative, genetic, or idiopathic hair cell and neural loss.
additionalDifferentials: Cerebellar ataxia and degenerative gait disorders
CANVAS (cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, vestibular areflexia syndrome)
Functional or multifactorial dizziness in older adults
Downbeat nystagmus syndromes from craniocervical junction pathology
additionalInvestigations: Bedside head impulse test and dynamic visual acuity assessment
Video head impulse testing to quantify vestibulo-ocular reflex gain in all canals
Caloric testing to confirm bilateral reduced responses
Rotational chair testing for low-frequency vestibular function
Audiometry to detect associated cochlear involvement
Neurological evaluation and imaging when ataxia or neuropathy suggests a central or systemic cause
redFlags: Progressive ataxia or neuropathy pointing to a central or systemic disorder
History of aminoglycoside exposure enabling prevention in others
Falls with injury from severe imbalance
Rapidly progressive course suggesting autoimmune or paraneoplastic disease
reference.prognosis: Peripheral vestibular function rarely recovers, but sustained vestibular rehabilitation improves gaze stability and gait, though oscillopsia and darkness-related unsteadiness often persist to some degree.
pitfalls: Attributing symptoms to non-specific dizziness and missing the diagnosis for years
Overlooking aminoglycoside ototoxicity as a preventable cause
Not testing both directions on the head impulse test
Failing to screen for CANVAS and other central or systemic associations
references: Barany Society Consensus: Diagnostic Criteria for Bilateral Vestibulopathy
management: Vestibular rehabilitation exercises promoting gaze stabilisation and sensory substitution as the mainstay of treatment
Identify and remove the cause, stopping and avoiding aminoglycoside and other ototoxic drugs and treating any bilateral Meniere disease
Corticosteroids or immunosuppression where an autoimmune aetiology is identified
Falls prevention through home-hazard reduction, adequate lighting, walking aids and advice about moving in the dark
Patient education to avoid situations that rely on vestibular input, such as swimming underwater and night driving
Audiovestibular and neurology referral to evaluate for a central or systemic cause when ataxia or neuropathy coexists
Consideration of an investigational vestibular implant in severe refractory disease
